title: Binary Search — never finds the last element

choices.text: The loop condition `lo < hi` exits before checking the final single-element range, so a target at the high end is missed.
`(lo + hi) >> 1` overflows for large arrays and computes the wrong midpoint.
`hi` should be initialized to `nums.length`, not `nums.length - 1`.
The comparison `nums[mid] < target` should be `nums[mid] <= target`.

explanation: With `lo < hi`, when the search space narrows to one element (`lo === hi`) the loop stops without testing `nums[lo]`. For target 5 in [1,3,5], lo and hi converge on index 2 but the loop never checks it. The fix is `while (lo <= hi)`.

title: Binary Search on Answer — midpoint overflows and loops forever
actual: INFINITE_LOOP (mid becomes negative once lo+hi exceeds 2^31, so lo never converges)

choices.text: `(lo + hi) >> 1` truncates the sum to a signed 32-bit integer; once `lo + hi` exceeds 2^31 the midpoint goes negative, so the range never converges.
The loop condition should be `lo < hi`; using `lo <= hi` causes one extra iteration that never terminates.
`ans` is uninitialized for the failing case, so the comparison `mid >= target` reads a stale accumulator.
The comparison should be `mid > target` instead of `mid >= target` to find the first qualifying value.

explanation: JavaScript numbers are 64-bit floats, but the bitwise `>>` operator first coerces its operands to signed 32-bit integers. When `lo + hi` exceeds 2,147,483,647 the result wraps to a negative `mid`, so `mid >= target` is false and `lo` is set to a negative value — the range can never close. The fix is `lo + ((hi - lo) >> 1)`, which never overflows because `hi - lo` stays in range.

title: Longest Substring — window shrinks on the wrong threshold

choices.text: The shrink condition `freq.get(c) > 2` permits one duplicate character inside the window, so the window is never narrowed when a repeat first appears.
`best` is initialized to 0 instead of 1, so single-character windows are undercounted.
The window mutates `freq` while iterating over it, skipping the element that should be removed.
`left` advances by one when it should advance to `right`, an off-by-one in the pointer update.

explanation: A 'no repeating characters' window is valid only when every count is 1. Shrinking while `freq.get(c) > 2` tolerates a character appearing twice, so for "abba" the window grows to the whole string (length 4) instead of stopping at 2. The fix is `while (freq.get(c) > 1)`.

title: Longest Substring — wrong initial best breaks empty input

choices.text: `best` is seeded with 1, so an empty string returns 1 even though the loop body never runs to correct it.
The loop should be `right <= s.length`; the off-by-one skips the final character.
The shrink condition `freq.get(c) > 1` is too strict and should be `>= 1`.
`left` is never reset between windows, so stale state from a previous call leaks in.

explanation: The accumulator `best` should start at the identity value 0 (a window of zero length). Seeding it with 1 assumes at least one character exists. For an empty string the `for` loop never executes, so the bogus initial 1 is returned instead of 0. The fix is `let best = 0`.

title: BFS — neighbors enqueued without a visited check

choices.text: Neighbors are enqueued unconditionally with no visited set, so in a cyclic graph nodes are re-enqueued forever.
Visited is marked on dequeue instead of on enqueue, allowing a few duplicate entries.
Using `queue.shift()` makes this a stack; it should use `queue.pop()` for breadth-first order.
`processed` starts at 0 when it should start at 1 to count the start node.

explanation: BFS must track which nodes have been discovered. With no visited array, every cycle (0→1→0→...) re-enqueues nodes endlessly. The fix is to maintain a `visited` array and only enqueue a neighbor when it has not yet been marked — marking it at the moment of enqueue.

title: BFS — marking visited on dequeue overcounts diamond paths

choices.text: Marking visited on dequeue leaves a node unmarked while it sits in the queue, so both parents in a diamond enqueue it and it is processed twice.
There is no visited array at all, so the traversal loops forever on the cycle.
`count` is initialized to 0 instead of 1, so the start node is undercounted.
`queue.shift()` returns elements in the wrong order, double-visiting the deepest node.

explanation: Node 3 has two parents (1 and 2). Because visited is set only when a node is dequeued, node 3 is still unmarked when node 1 enqueues it AND when node 2 enqueues it — so it lands in the queue twice and is counted twice (5 instead of 4). The fix is to mark a node visited at the moment you enqueue it.

title: Reverse Linked List — overwrites next before saving it
actual: 1 (the rest of the list is lost)

choices.text: `curr.next` is reassigned to `prev` before the original next node is saved, so `curr = curr.next` walks backward instead of forward and the tail is dropped.
`prev` should be initialized to `head` instead of `null`, causing the first node to be lost.
The loop condition `while (curr)` should be `while (curr.next)`, an off-by-one that skips the last node.
Reversing mutates the list while iterating it, so nodes are visited out of order.

explanation: Reversal needs a temporary to hold the next node before rewiring: `const next = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`. Here `curr.next = prev` runs first, so the subsequent `curr = curr.next` reads the pointer that was just overwritten and the traversal collapses after the first node, returning just `1`.

title: Cycle Detection — fast pointer moves one step, not two

choices.text: `fast` advances by one node, the same speed as `slow`, so they stay pointer-equal every iteration and report a cycle even on an acyclic list.
`slow` and `fast` are both initialized to `head`, so they start equal and the very first comparison is a false positive.
The loop condition is missing a visited set, so each node is revisited and falsely flagged.
The comparison should be `slow.val === fast.val`; comparing node references is the bug.

explanation: Floyd's algorithm relies on the fast pointer moving twice as fast as the slow pointer. With `fast = fast.next` they advance in lockstep, so after each step `slow === fast` is trivially true and the function reports a cycle on a straight, acyclic list. The fix is `fast = fast.next.next`. (Note both starting at `head` is fine — the comparison happens after advancing.)

title: Climbing Stairs — zero base case halves every answer

choices.text: `dp[0]` is the count of ways to reach the ground, which must be 1; setting it to 0 drops one path from every state built on it.
The loop should start at `i = 1`, an off-by-one that skips a base step.
`dp` should be initialized to `Infinity` so unreachable states are excluded.
The recurrence should be `dp[i] = dp[i-1] * dp[i-2]`; using addition undercounts the paths.

explanation: There is exactly one way to be standing at step 0 (take no steps), so `dp[0]` must be 1. With `dp[0] = 0`, `dp[2] = dp[1] + dp[0] = 1` and `dp[3] = dp[2] + dp[1] = 2` instead of the correct 3. The fix is `dp[0] = 1`.

title: Coin Change — zero-filled table reports impossible amounts as solvable

choices.text: Unreachable subproblems are pre-filled with 0 instead of Infinity, so `Math.min` always prefers the bogus 0 and impossible amounts look free.
The inner loop has an off-by-one; `a - c >= 0` should be `a - c > 0`, dropping the exact-change case.
The coins array is mutated during iteration, so the denomination 2 is skipped.
`dp[0]` should be Infinity, not 0; the base case is inverted.

explanation: For a min-coins table, every state except `dp[0]` must start at Infinity so that `Math.min` only adopts a value when a real coin reaches it. Filled with 0, `dp[3] = min(0, dp[1] + 1) = 0` even though 3 cannot be made from 2s — so it returns 0 instead of -1. The fix is `new Array(amount + 1).fill(Infinity)` with `dp[0] = 0`.

title: Frequency Map — incrementing an undefined slot yields NaN

choices.text: On the first occurrence of each character `map[c]` is `undefined`, and `undefined + 1` is `NaN`, which then poisons every later increment of that key.
Using a plain object instead of a Map causes prototype keys to collide, producing the wrong counts.
The loop mutates `map` while iterating `s`, skipping the second 'a'.
Characters are compared by reference, so distinct 'a' characters are counted separately.

explanation: The accumulator is never seeded. The first time a character is seen, `map[c]` is `undefined`, and `undefined + 1` evaluates to `NaN`; every subsequent `NaN + 1` stays `NaN`. The fix is to default the slot: `map[c] = (map[c] ?? 0) + 1`.

title: Remove Value — splicing while iterating skips elements

choices.text: `splice` shifts every later element one index left, but `i` still advances, so the element that moved into the current slot is never examined.
The comparison `nums[i] === val` should be `nums[i] == val`; strict equality skips a coercible duplicate.
The loop bound `i < nums.length` is read once at the start, an off-by-one that stops early.
`splice(i, 1)` should be `splice(i, 0)`; the deletion count is wrong.

explanation: Removing index 0 shifts the second 2 into index 0, but the loop then increments to index 1, jumping past it. So one 2 survives and the result is [2, 3] instead of [3]. The fix is to decrement `i` after a splice (`i--`), iterate backward, or build a new filtered array instead of mutating during the forward scan.

title: Top-K Largest — comparator sorts the wrong direction

choices.text: The comparator `(a, b) => a - b` sorts ascending, so `slice(0, k)` takes the k smallest values instead of the k largest.
`slice(0, k)` is an off-by-one; it should be `slice(0, k + 1)` to include the kth element.
Spreading into a new array mutates the original during the sort, corrupting the order.
The accumulator is uninitialized, so the first comparison reads an undefined element.

explanation: A min-heap top-k keeps the largest by evicting the smallest; the equivalent sort must be descending. `(a, b) => a - b` sorts ascending, so the first k entries are the smallest — [1, 2] instead of [4, 3]. The fix is `(a, b) => b - a` (the order within the returned k may vary, but it must contain the largest values).
